crime.value: A fake protection racket: an invented criminal syndicate ('The Big Ones') extorts a 5% dues increase from the Montevideo taxi drivers' union, backed by staged 'accidents' — a bombed cab, sabotaged brakes, sugar in a fuel tank, a self-inflicted knife wound. Central question posed to the drivers: who are The Big Ones and can they be resisted? (Reader question: who is really behind it?)
crime.quote: "Protection, you fool. The Big Ones are offering to protect you from the many accidents that could easily happen to you."

victim.value: The rank-and-file taxi drivers — Diego Camero (cab blown up), Pepa Lopez (brakes cut), Joaquin Celestinos (blackjacked, tank sugared) — chosen as expendable demonstrations because they were trusting fellow members; ultimately the whole membership, milked monthly. Later victim: Manoël the actor, killed for demanding a bigger cut.
victim.quote: "Diego Camero's cab was blown up this morning... How will he now provide for his family?"

closed_world.value: The Montevideo Taxicab Drivers Association — its shabby headquarters above a sidewalk cafe off Plaza Independencia, its three officers, and the city's cab ranks, casino and waterfront; police excluded by the threat of informers.
closed_world.quote: "the shabby room above a sidewalk cafe that serves us as permanent union headquarters"

culprit_and_motive.value: Fernando Quintana, the association's own secretary and narrator, with Manoël — a deported-risk bit-player actor working illegally as a croupier — hired to impersonate the Big Ones' emissary. Motive: a perpetual monthly income skimmed from his fellow drivers' dues, split 75/25 (later reversed under blackmail).
culprit_and_motive.quote: "Twenty-five percent for you and seventy-five for me. That was our agreement."

resolution.value: No official justice: the fraud succeeds, the union votes the dues increase and passes it to fares. 'Order' is restored only by Fernando silencing his blackmailing accomplice — wiring plastic explosive to Manoël's Volvo ignition.
resolution.quote: "wired enough plastic explosive under its dashboard to blow a dozen Volvos and their occupants into tiny bits"

investigator.value: Fernando Quintana, first-person narrator posing as a loyal victim-officer investigating The Big Ones — in fact the criminal himself; an inverted/unreliable-narrator lens with no true detective.
investigator.quote: "Follow him, Fernando! See where he goes."

suspect_architecture.value: Not a whodunit cast; the 'suspects' are the association officers and the mysterious extortionist. Cast: Carlos Olavide (head, credulous authority), Luis Bayeu (segundo, muscle), Fernando Quintana (secretary, narrator and secret architect of the fraud), and 'Manoël Goncalves' (in fact a down-at-heel actor turned croupier, Fernando's hired accomplice). Victims Diego Camero, Pepa Lopez, Joaquin Celestinos serve as corroborating casualties.
suspect_architecture.quote: Carlos Olavide, head of your association. Luis Bayeu, segundo. Fernando Quintana, secretary.

red_herring.value: The whole 'Big Ones' criminal syndicate is a fabricated red herring — a mythical international crime guild Carlos half-remembers, plus staged 'accidents' (Fernando's self-inflicted throat cut, the dwarf-and-tall-man holdup, the bombed cab, cut brakes, sugar in a fuel tank) designed to point at nonexistent gangsters.
red_herring.quote: A dwarf and a tall man wearing a beige hat are supposed to have held me up and cut my throat, as a warning from The Big Ones.

clue_fairness.value: Clues are planted in plain sight before the confession: the Portuguese accent shared by 'Goncalves' and the alleged dwarf, the fat man's silent ascent but heavy descent, the lean-faced driver of the battered Volvo, and Fernando's convenient hospital call opening the story.
clue_fairness.quote: the driver turned his head my way, and I saw his face was not full and fleshy like Goncalves', but lean, far too lean.

social_world.value: Uruguayan working-class union politics: the Montevideo Taxicab Drivers Association's hierarchy (head, segundo, secretary) and its trust in officers; police corruption alleged; costs passed on to the public via fare increases; immigrant precarity (forged work permit) creating leverage.
social_world.quote: We also voted to raise taxi fares five percent, you see.

alibi.value: Fernando's alibi is his own victimhood — the hospital, five stitches, and the doctor deceived with a clothesline story make him seem a target rather than the perpetrator; 'Goncalves' hides behind disguise and a false identity.
alibi.quote: I told him I almost tore my head off by walking into my wife's steel clothesline in the back yard. He believed me.

reveal_mechanic.value: A confessional two-hander in the hotel garden: the croupier accomplice itemizes his disguise (gray contact lenses, wax cheek wads, Falstaff midriff padding) while Fernando counts out the 75/25 split, demonstrating the fraud rather than stating it.
reveal_mechanic.quote: And the wax wads in my cheeks to make my face fat? And the midriff padding I used to wear when I played Falstaff?

media_and_audience.value: Perception is manufactured via the tape recording played to the membership, plus the displayed knife wound and testimonies of 'accidents' — the audience of drivers is scripted into believing in a mafia and voting the dues increase.
media_and_audience.quote: He played the tape of our meeting with Goncalves, turning the volume up full so that all of us could hear

investigator_wound.value: The narrator-schemer's vulnerability is greed and exposure: mutual blackmail with the accomplice, who deports easily while Fernando would be killed by his own drivers — the pressure drives him to plant explosive in the Volvo.
investigator_wound.quote: But you, my friend, would be killed by your own cabdrivers before the police could intervene to save you!

victims_enemies.value: The real victims are the rank-and-file cabdrivers — Diego Camero (twelve children, one good arm), Pepa Lopez, Joaquin Celestinos — betrayed not by an outside gang but by their own association secretary, Fernando Quintana, a trusted colleague who sabotaged their livelihoods. Secondary victim: Manoël, the accomplice-actor whose greed makes him Fernando's enemy at the end.
victims_enemies.quote: "They might as well have killed him as destroyed his taxicab. How will he now provide for his family?"

suspect_wounds.value: Fernando disguises himself as a victim by cutting his own throat, using his visible wound to deflect all suspicion; Manoël's vulnerability is that he is an illegal immigrant working under an assumed name on a forged permit, which makes him exposable and expendable.
suspect_wounds.quote: "a down-at-heels actor turned croupier, who entered Uruguay illegally and is now working... on a forged work permit"

unreliable_frame.value: The entire story is narrated by Fernando Quintana, the culprit, in first person — his opening hospital phone call, his outrage at the letter, his 'shaken nerves' are all performance for the reader as much as for Carlos. Manoël's account is equally false, being an actor's role.
unreliable_frame.quote: "I actually cut my own throat, Manoël. It bled all over my shirt."

setting_as_constraint.value: Montevideo's insular taxi-driver union culture is the constraint and the weapon: the drivers cannot go to the police (told there are informers), the association's closed membership vote is the only mechanism for money, and dues collected in cash monthly give the culprit a permanent, untraceable income stream. Casino gardens at Carasco provide the anonymous handover point.
setting_as_constraint.quote: "If any of you goes to the police, I'll know it within thirty minutes. And you'll be dead men within twenty-four hours."

evidence_type.value: Testimonial/documentary theatre used as false evidence rather than true detection: the extortion letter and, above all, the tape recording of the 'Goncalves' interview, played to the membership alongside physical exhibits (the stitched cut, the wrecked cabs) to manufacture belief.
evidence_type.quote: "A tape recorder. You'll need a record of this conversation."

false_suspect.value: 'The Big Ones' / 'The Corporation' — a wholly fictitious criminal syndicate, embodied by the invented Manoël Goncalves, on whom all blame for the sabotage is placed.
false_suspect.quote: "The Big Ones, we are called, or The Corporation. You have heard of us, perhaps?"

technical_detail.value: Stagecraft and sabotage know-how: gray contact lenses, wax wads in the cheeks and Falstaff midriff padding to build the fat man; plus brake tampering, sugar in a gasoline tank, and plastic explosive wired to a Volvo ignition.
technical_detail.quote: "the wax wads in my cheeks to make my face fat? And the midriff padding I used to wear when I played Falstaff?"

moral_ambiguity.value: Little moral defense — Fernando is a trusted union officer who preys on his own poor colleagues; the only mitigation offered is comic craftsmanship (his self-inflicted wound, the elegance of the scheme) and the fact that the cost was passed to consumers via a fare rise, so drivers lose nothing. His final murder of the blackmailing Manoël is greed answering greed.
moral_ambiguity.quote: "We passed the increase along to the consumer, as usual. We also voted to raise taxi fares five percent, you see."
